docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
msflib-auth issues access tokens and gives your host app the FastAPI dependencies that identify the caller. It covers password login, logout (token revocation), password recovery, optional Google OAuth, and two dependency factories: one that resolves the current account from a bearer token, and one that resolves the current workspace and the account's membership in it.

It does not define your account or workspace models. You pass them in, typically the ones from msflib-account and msflib-workspaces.

For the end-to-end picture of how a request becomes a scoped identity, see Scopes, tenancy and workspaces.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
[tool.poetry.dependencies]
msflib = { git = "https://github.com/msflib/fastapi.git", subdirectory = "core", rev = "core-v0.2.1" }
msflib-auth = { git = "https://github.com/msflib/fastapi.git", subdirectory = "modules/auth", rev = "auth-v0.2.2" }

The package depends on authlib and itsdangerous. It imports no other MSFLib module, so it works with any SQLModel account model that has email, hashed_password and status columns.

msflib/auth/__init__.py exports nothing. Import from the submodules: msflib.auth.deps, msflib.auth.router, msflib.auth.resolvers, msflib.auth.config, msflib.auth.eventbus.

docs.title: Wiring into a host app
docs.text:
Build the dependency namespaces once at startup, then mount the router.

from fastapi import FastAPI
from msflib.auth.deps import get_account_dependencies, get_user_dependencies
from msflib.auth.resolvers import PathParameterResolver
from msflib.auth.router import router as auth_router

account_deps = get_account_dependencies(
    AccountModel=Account,
    oauth_token_url="/api/v1/auth/login",
    secret_key=settings.SECRET_KEY,
    session_dep=get_session,
    keystore_dep=get_keystore,
)

# Only needed when your app has workspaces.
user_deps = get_user_dependencies(
    UserModel=User,
    WorkspaceModel=Workspace,
    session_dep=get_session,
    account_dependencies=account_deps,
    workspace_resolver=PathParameterResolver(),
)

app = FastAPI()
app.include_router(
    auth_router(
        get_session=get_session,
        get_keystore=get_keystore,
        get_current_account=account_deps.get_current_account,
        account_type=Account,
        account_read_type=AccountRead,
        settings=settings,
        prefix="/api/v1/auth",
    )
)

What you supply:

Argument Meaning session_dep / get_session A FastAPI dependency yielding a SQLModel Session. keystore_dep / get_keystore A dependency returning a StoreInterface (for example msflib.core.store.MapStore). Used to record revoked accounts. secret_key The key that signs and verifies JWTs. Use the same value as settings.SECRET_KEY; the router signs with the latter. settings Your settings object. The router reads the AUTH namespace from it and SECRET_KEY as a flat attribute (settings.SECRET_KEY).

Known issue (#287)

The router reads settings.SECRET_KEY from the top level of the settings object. With fully composed settings (core only under CORE, as in the quick-start layout) POST /auth/login and the password reset endpoints raise AttributeError, although get_account_dependencies(secret_key=settings.scope("CORE").SECRET_KEY) itself works. Mix CoreSettings into your settings class (class Settings(CoreSettings, SettingsBase), with the other modules still nested) so SECRET_KEY is a top-level attribute.

get_account_dependencies also accepts active_statuses (default ["active", "online"]) and account_role_attr (default "role"). get_user_dependencies accepts user_role_attr (default "type"), current_workspace_attr (default "current_workspace_id") and workspace_resolver.

docs.title: Routes added by the router
docs.text:
Route (under the prefix) Behaviour POST /login OAuth2 password form (username is the email). Returns access_token, expires, token_type, account and user. DELETE /logout Revokes the caller's token. POST /password-recovery Emails a reset link and a short code. POST /verify-token Checks a reset token or a short code plus email. POST /reset-password Sets a new password from a valid reset token. GET /google/login, POST /google/callback Google OAuth. Return 403 unless ENABLE_GOOGLE_OAUTH is true.

The router takes optional hooks: access_token_claims_decorator(account, context) adds claims to the JWT, access_token_decorator(payload, context) rewrites the login response, send_reset_pwd_email_override replaces the recovery email sender, access_token_response_type replaces the Token response model, and auth_payload_type validates extra data a client sends to the Google callback.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Settings live in the AUTH namespace (msflib.auth.config.AuthSettings).

Key Default Notes ACCESS_TOKEN_EXPIRE_MINUTES 30 Lifetime of tokens issued at login. EMAIL_RESET_TOKEN_EXPIRE_HOURS 48 Lifetime of password reset tokens and codes. PASSWORD_RESET_PATH /reset Appended to CORE.CLIENT_HOST in the reset email link. ENABLE_GOOGLE_OAUTH False Enables the Google routes. ALLOW_GOOGLE_OAUTH_SIGNUP False Create an account for an unknown Google email. Requires a listener for google-account-create. GOOGLE_OAUTH_CLIENT_ID, GOOGLE_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET empty Read when the router is built. GOOGLE_REDIRECT_URI empty Default redirect when the client does not send one.

How you set these from the environment depends on how you compose settings:

  • Subclassed (class Settings(AuthSettings, CoreSettings, SettingsBase), as used by the repository's test site): use the flat field name, for example ACCESS_TOKEN_EXPIRE_MINUTES=60.
  • Composed style (AUTH: AuthSettings = AuthSettings() as a field): use the nested form, AUTH__ACCESS_TOKEN_EXPIRE_MINUTES=60. The flat names also work for every key in the table above.

Either way, code reads values with settings.scope("AUTH").

Behaviour may change (#280)

The nested NS__KEY environment style only works for composed (field) settings, not for subclassed hosts. Use the flat field name with subclassed settings, as described above.

docs.title: Account dependencies
docs.text:
get_account_dependencies(...) returns a namespace with:

Member Behaviour get_current_account Decodes the bearer token, rejects it with 401 if invalid or revoked, loads the account by email == token.sub, and 404s if it does not exist. get_current_account_or_none Same, but returns None when no token is sent. For endpoints that serve both anonymous and signed-in callers. get_current_active_account Also requires account.status in active_statuses; otherwise 401. get_current_active_superuser Also requires account.role == "root"; otherwise 403. This check is hard-coded and ignores account_role_attr (see the notice below). RoleCheck(roles) A callable class for dependencies=[Depends(RoleCheck([...]))]. Passes only when the account's role attribute is in roles; otherwise 403. It does not check the account's status; add Depends(get_current_active_account) to require an active account.

Known issue (#272)

get_current_active_superuser hard-codes account.role == "root" and ignores account_role_attr. If your role attribute or superuser role differs, require both get_current_active_account and RoleCheck([...]) with the roles you want. RoleCheck alone depends on get_current_account, so it also admits inactive accounts that have a matching role.

RoleCheck is an exact membership test. RoleCheck(["admin"]) does not admit root; list every role you want to allow.

RoleCheck and WorkspaceRoleCheck compare a role attribute and read nothing else. For roles that admins create and assign at runtime, tiers and permissions, use the guards in authz; msflib-auth does not depend on it.

docs.title: Workspace resolution
docs.text:
get_user_dependencies(...) turns a request into a workspace and a membership. The strategy for finding the workspace is a WorkspaceResolver, chosen once at startup.

A resolver receives a ResolverContext (session, account, path_params, headers) and returns a workspace slug, or None when the request does not identify one. Header keys in headers are lower-case. Two resolvers ship in msflib.auth.resolvers:

Resolver Reads Default PathParameterResolver(param_name=...) A path parameter workspace_slug HttpHeaderResolver(header_name=...) A request header X-Workspace

If you pass no resolver, PathParameterResolver() is used. HttpHeaderResolver also declares the header as an optional parameter on the dependencies, so it shows up in OpenAPI.

Once the resolver returns a slug, the dependency looks the workspace up:

  • default resolves to the workspace with is_default = True. If none exists, the dependency returns None rather than raising.
  • current resolves to the workspace whose id is account.current_workspace_id. It is a 404 for anonymous callers and for accounts with no current workspace.
  • Any other value is matched against Workspace.slug; 404 if not found.
  • None from the resolver is a 404 with "No workspace specified."

The namespace then exposes:

Member Behaviour get_current_workspace Requires an authenticated account (get_current_account), then resolves the workspace as above. get_current_workspace_anonymous Same resolution without authentication. get_current_user Finds the UserModel row with account_id == account.id and workspace_id == workspace.id. A missing row is a 403: authenticated, but not a member of this workspace. get_current_active_user Also requires user.status == "active"; otherwise 401. WorkspaceRoleCheck(roles) Passes when the membership's role attribute (type by default) is in roles; otherwise 403.

Behaviour may change (#269)

get_current_workspace_anonymous does no membership or status check. It only maps a slug to a workspace row. Use it for deliberately public reads, and do not return anything from it that a non-member should not see.

Membership is the only path to a workspace. get_current_user never grants access because the account owns the tenant or has a platform role; the account needs a membership row in that specific workspace. See workspaces for how rows are created.

docs.title: A custom resolver
docs.text:
Subclass WorkspaceResolver for any other strategy, such as a subdomain or a claim on the account:

from msflib.auth.resolvers import ResolverContext, WorkspaceResolver


class SubdomainResolver(WorkspaceResolver):
    def resolve(self, context: ResolverContext) -> str | None:
        host = context.headers.get("host", "")
        return host.split(".")[0] if host.count(".") >= 2 else None

Pass an instance as workspace_resolver=. A resolver is a plain synchronous object, so it is easy to unit-test with a hand-built ResolverContext.

One resolver applies to everything built by one get_user_dependencies call. To use two strategies in one app, call the factory twice and use each namespace on its own routers.

docs.title: Token revocation
docs.text: Tokens are JWTs whose sub is the account email. Logout stores the email in the keystore, and get_current_account rejects any token whose sub is in the keystore. Revocation therefore applies to the account rather than to individual tokens, and logging in again clears it. If you need to end a single session, put a unique claim in the token with access_token_claims_decorator and check it in your own dependency.

docs.title: Events
docs.text:
Event names are in msflib.auth.eventbus.EventName:

Event Emitted when account-logged-in A login or Google callback succeeds. Optional: no listener is fine. google-account-create A Google login names an unknown email and ALLOW_GOOGLE_OAUTH_SIGNUP is true. Required: a listener must create the account, or the callback returns 500.

Register the listener on the app emitter, for example @app_emitter.on("google-account-create") with app_emitter = bind_app_emitter(app). A listener added with emitter.on(...) at import time lands on the default emitter, which the router does not see, and the callback returns 500 "No listener". Sync and async listeners on the app emitter both work.

See Event bus for registering listeners.

docs.title: Protect routes by account role and workspace membership
docs.text:
This runs against an in-memory SQLite database using the models from msflib-account and msflib-workspaces. member and guest are workspace roles; the owner passes WorkspaceRoleCheck.

from datetime import timedelta

from fastapi import Depends, FastAPI
from fastapi.testclient import TestClient
from msflib.account.models.account import Account
from msflib.auth.deps import get_account_dependencies, get_user_dependencies
from msflib.auth.resolvers import PathParameterResolver
from msflib.core.security import create_access_token
from msflib.core.store import MapStore
from msflib.workspaces.models import UserType
from msflib.workspaces.models.user import User
from msflib.workspaces.models.workspace import Workspace

# get_session, get_keystore and SECRET_KEY come from your app; see "Wiring".
account_deps = get_account_dependencies(
    AccountModel=Account,
    oauth_token_url="/login",
    secret_key=SECRET_KEY,
    session_dep=get_session,
    keystore_dep=get_keystore,
)
user_deps = get_user_dependencies(
    UserModel=User,
    WorkspaceModel=Workspace,
    session_dep=get_session,
    account_dependencies=account_deps,
    workspace_resolver=PathParameterResolver(),
)

app = FastAPI()


@app.get("/{workspace_slug}/whoami")
def whoami(
    workspace=Depends(user_deps.get_current_workspace),
    user=Depends(user_deps.get_current_active_user),
):
    return {"workspace": workspace.slug, "user_id": user.id, "type": user.type}


@app.get(
    "/{workspace_slug}/admin",
    dependencies=[Depends(user_deps.WorkspaceRoleCheck([UserType.owner, UserType.admin]))],
)
def admin_only():
    return {"ok": True}


@app.get("/{workspace_slug}/public")
def public(workspace=Depends(user_deps.get_current_workspace_anonymous)):
    return {"workspace": workspace.slug}


token = create_access_token("ada@example.com", SECRET_KEY, timedelta(minutes=5))
client = TestClient(app)
client.get("/acme/whoami", headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {token}"})
# 200 {"workspace": "acme", "user_id": 1, "type": "owner"}   (ada is a member)
# 403 {"detail": "User not found in specified workspace"}    (a non-member)
# GET /nope/public -> 404 "Workspace not found"

docs.title: Resolve the workspace from a header
docs.text:
from msflib.auth.resolvers import HttpHeaderResolver

user_deps = get_user_dependencies(
    UserModel=User,
    WorkspaceModel=Workspace,
    session_dep=get_session,
    account_dependencies=account_deps,
    workspace_resolver=HttpHeaderResolver("X-Workspace"),
)

Routes no longer carry a {workspace_slug} path segment. A client sends X-Workspace: acme; without the header the dependency responds 404 "No workspace specified.". X-Workspace: current selects the account's current_workspace_id, and X-Workspace: default the default workspace.

docs.title: Add claims and extra response fields at login
docs.text:
The response model filters what the login route returns, so extra fields need a response type that declares them.

from msflib.auth.models import Token


class LoginResponse(Token):
    environment: str = ""


app.include_router(
    auth_router(
        get_session=get_session,
        get_keystore=get_keystore,
        get_current_account=account_deps.get_current_account,
        account_type=Account,
        account_read_type=AccountRead,
        settings=settings,
        access_token_response_type=LoginResponse,
        access_token_claims_decorator=lambda account, ctx: {
            "email_domain": account.email.split("@")[1]
        },
        access_token_decorator=lambda payload, ctx: {**payload, "environment": "staging"},
    )
)

ctx is {"session": session}. The JWT now carries an email_domain claim and the login body includes environment. The workspaces module ships WorkspaceAction.build_access_token_claims and decorate_access_token_payload, which are designed for these two hooks and add the active workspace and membership.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Cause and fix 401 "Could not validate credentials" The token is malformed, expired, or signed with a different key. secret_key passed to get_account_dependencies must equal settings.SECRET_KEY used by the router. 401 "Token expired" right after logout Expected: logout revoked the account. A new login clears it. 404 "No workspace specified." The resolver returned None: the path parameter name does not match the route, or the header is missing. 404 "Current workspace unknown for anonymous user." The slug current was used on an anonymous dependency. 403 "User not found in specified workspace" The account has no membership row in that workspace. Create one (see workspaces). 403 on an admin route for a root account RoleCheck and WorkspaceRoleCheck match exactly. Add root to the list, or use get_current_active_superuser. Google callback returns 500 "No listener for Google account creation" ALLOW_GOOGLE_OAUTH_SIGNUP is on but nothing listens to google-account-create. Register a listener that creates the account. Reset email contains the wrong link host The link is CORE.CLIENT_HOST plus AUTH.PASSWORD_RESET_PATH. Set both.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
msflib-authz stores roles and their permissions in the database and assigns them to accounts at runtime. It answers two questions:

  • Does this account hold permission X here? (RoleService.has_permission, the require_permission guard)
  • Which roles does this account hold here? (RoleService.get_role_keys_for, the require_role guard)

It sits beside the simple role attributes (Account.role, User.type) that auth guards compare, rather than replacing them. Apps pick either way, or both; see Two ways to guard a route and Legacy roles. msflib-auth does not depend on this module.

The terms tier, owner and assignment scope are easy to confuse because they all mention tenants and workspaces. Read Three questions about a role before the rest.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
[tool.poetry.dependencies]
msflib = { git = "https://github.com/msflib/fastapi.git", subdirectory = "core", rev = "core-v0.2.2" }
msflib-tenancy = { git = "https://github.com/msflib/fastapi.git", subdirectory = "modules/tenancy", rev = "tenancy-v0.2.1" }
msflib-authz = { git = "https://github.com/msflib/fastapi.git", subdirectory = "modules/authz", rev = "authz-v<version>" }

Use the release tag of the version you want; do not pin dev. The package depends on core and tenancy. Its names load lazily, so importing msflib.authz does not register the table models; import msflib.authz.models before you create tables.

docs.title: Wiring into a host app
docs.text:
1. Add the role, role_permission, role_assignment, group, group_member and resource_access tables to your schema. An app that already created the first three must add group and group_member before it upgrades: role and permission checks read group_member to expand a user's groups, so they fail with a missing-table error until it exists. The package ships no migrations: import msflib.authz.models before SQLModel.metadata.create_all, or include the tables in your own migrations (see How a module is wired). An app that created group from the groups release also has group.workspace_id as NOT NULL, and create_all never alters an existing column. Make it nullable before you create a group with workspace_id=None (the workspace-agnostic bucket); on PostgreSQL that is ALTER TABLE "group" ALTER COLUMN workspace_id DROP NOT NULL.
  2. Register permission keys at import time.
  3. Seed the system roles at startup, after every module has registered its keys.
  4. Build the guards with get_authz_dependencies and protect routes with require_permission or require_role.

docs.title: Register permission keys
docs.text:
from msflib.authz import PERMISSION_REGISTRY

PERMISSION_REGISTRY.register("documents.share", tenant_cascade=True)

tenant_cascade decides whether a tenant-tier role grants the permission inside a workspace. A permission that should only ever be held through workspace membership leaves it off.

tiers limits which roles may hold a key (default: any). authz.manage_roles is registered for the platform and tenant tiers only. A role of another tier is ignored for that key during resolution, however the key reached it (including a prefix.* wildcard), and add_permissions rejects an exact key the role's tier may not hold. The seeded workspace roles leave such keys out.

PERMISSION_REGISTRY.register("ops.reset", tiers=(RoleTier.platform,))

Registering the same key twice is fine unless tenant_cascade or tiers differ, which raises ValueError.

docs.title: Seeding
docs.text:
from msflib.authz.seed import (
    backfill_account_role_assignments,
    seed_role_permissions,
    seed_system_roles,
)

roles = seed_system_roles(session, default_tenant_id=tenant_id)
seed_role_permissions(session, roles=roles)  # after every module has registered its keys
backfill_account_role_assignments(
    session, roles=roles, default_tenant_id=tenant_id, accounts=[(a.id, a.role) for a in accounts]
)
Seeded role Tier Owner Permissions root platform none every registered key a platform role may hold admin tenant default tenant every registered key a tenant role may hold user tenant default tenant none owner, admin workspace none (template) every key a workspace role may hold (so not authz.manage_roles, nor a prefix.* key covering it) member, guest workspace none (template) none

All the seeders are idempotent, safe to run from several processes at once, and run on every startup. Each is one unit of work and commits once at the end. seed_system_roles refuses, with RoleExistsError, to adopt a custom role that already holds a seeded identity (same key, tier and owner), and commits nothing in that case.

The backfills mirror the legacy attributes into assignments with source="legacy_backfill". The source is part of an assignment's identity: a runtime grant and the mirror of the same role are two rows, so a runtime grant (even an expired one) never blocks, renews or revokes the mirror, and the backfill never touches a runtime row. Callers cannot set the source: grant and ensure_assignment always write runtime rows.

  • backfill_account_role_assignments mirrors (account_id, Account.role): root as a platform assignment, admin and user as tenant assignments in the default tenant.
  • backfill_workspace_membership_role_assignments mirrors (account_id, workspace_id, tenant_id, User.type) as workspace assignments. It is not wired into the test site because that app has no workspace model; pass it your memberships.

Pass the complete set

A backfill treats its input as the whole truth. It revokes every legacy_backfill assignment the input no longer implies, including those of accounts or memberships that are missing from it, which is how deleted accounts and removed memberships lose their mirrored role. A partial list therefore revokes too much. An empty list does nothing, so a snapshot that failed to load cannot revoke every mirror; the stale mirrors of a table that really became empty must be revoked by hand. Runtime grants (source="runtime") are never touched.

Both backfills are transitional and go away once assignments replace the legacy attributes.

docs.title: require_permission
docs.text:
get_authz_dependencies(session_dep=..., tenancy_settings=..., get_current_account=..., get_current_workspace=..., get_current_active_user=..., get_current_tenant=...) returns a namespace with require_permission(key, tier=...):

authz = get_authz_dependencies(
    session_dep=get_session,
    tenancy_settings=settings.scope("TENANCY"),
    get_current_account=account_deps.get_current_account,
    get_current_workspace=user_deps.get_current_workspace,
    get_current_tenant=get_current_tenant,
)

router.get(
    "/{workspace_slug}/docs",
    dependencies=[Depends(authz.require_permission("documents.share"))],  # workspace tier
)
router.get(
    "/tenant-settings",
    dependencies=[Depends(authz.require_permission("documents.share", tier="tenant"))],
)
router.get(
    "/ops",
    dependencies=[Depends(authz.require_permission("authz.manage_roles", tier="platform"))],
)
  • The default tier is workspace. Workspace guards resolve the workspace from the request; tenant and platform guards never do.
  • An unknown tier raises ValueError when the dependency is built.
  • tier="platform" is satisfied only by platform-tier roles.
  • With get_current_tenant, the guard uses the request's tenant, and a request with no tenant is denied. Without it, the tenancy namespace's get_current_tenant supplies the default tenant from tenancy_settings.
  • A workspace that belongs to a different tenant than the request is denied.
  • Workspace guards need get_current_workspace, and identify the account from the workspace-and-active-user pair when both are passed, otherwise from get_current_account. Building a workspace guard without get_current_workspace raises ValueError, so a misconfigured app fails at startup instead of denying every request. Tenant and platform guards need get_current_account.

A guard passes when the caller holds a role, at a tier that reaches the request, that bundles the key (or a prefix.* key covering it):

Guard tier Satisfied by workspace (default) a workspace-tier role held in this workspace; a tenant-tier role of the request's tenant, only if the key is registered tenant_cascade=True; a platform-tier role tenant a tenant-tier role of the request's tenant; a platform-tier role platform a platform-tier role only

Denied, with 403, when:

  • the key is not registered in this process (a warning is logged, so a typo never grants). A bundled key that is no longer registered counts for nothing either, so every process that checks permissions, including workers and CLIs, must import the modules that register the keys;
  • no account can be identified, or a wired get_current_tenant returns no tenant;
  • the workspace belongs to another tenant, or a workspace guard has no workspace in the request;
  • the matching assignment is expired, or its scope does not fit its role's tier.

Prefer require_permission for new code: a permission names what may be done, and does not depend on what the roles happen to be called. Use require_role when the route is about holding a role.

To check a permission outside a route, for example inside a service, call RoleService.has_permission with the account, tenant and (for workspace permissions) workspace (see How a permission is resolved).

docs.title: require_role
docs.text:
Depends(authz.require_role(RoleKey(tier, key), ...)) passes when the caller holds any of the roles. Each key is matched at its own tier: a platform role anywhere, a tenant role in the request's tenant, a workspace role in the request's workspace.

from msflib.authz import RoleKey, RoleTier

router.get(
    "/ops",
    dependencies=[Depends(authz.require_role(RoleKey(RoleTier.platform, "root")))],
)
router.get(
    "/{workspace_slug}/admin",
    dependencies=[
        Depends(
            authz.require_role(
                RoleKey(RoleTier.workspace, "admin"), RoleKey(RoleTier.tenant, "admin")
            )
        )
    ],
)
  • It takes RoleKey only. A bare string raises TypeError when the dependency is built, and no keys raises ValueError.
  • The same key at another tier does not satisfy it: a tenant admin is not a workspace admin.
  • A guard with a workspace-tier key needs a workspace in the request and denies without one. Tenant and platform keys never resolve a workspace.
  • Tenant and workspace handling is the same as for require_permission: the request's tenant (denied when missing), a workspace of another tenant denied, account identified from the membership pair or get_current_account.
  • A tenant-tier key is held at a workspace route too: a tenant admin passes require_role(RoleKey(RoleTier.tenant, "admin")) on a workspace route. Unlike require_permission, there is no tenant_cascade switch, because the caller named the tenant role explicitly.
  • It reads assignments only. The legacy attributes do not count (see Legacy roles).

Prefer require_permission where the guard names an action, and require_role where it names a role.

docs.title: Two ways to guard a route
docs.text:
msflib-auth msflib-authz Guards RoleCheck, WorkspaceRoleCheck require_permission, require_role Reads Account.role, User.type attributes role assignments in the database Needs nothing beyond your account and user models the six authz tables, seeding Granularity a role name, exact match tier, owner and scope; permissions bundled into roles Changed at runtime by editing the attribute by granting or revoking assignments

Both are supported. Use auth when a role attribute is enough. Use authz when you need roles that admins create and assign at runtime, per-workspace or per-tenant roles, or permissions. The module routers that take a role guard parameter (role_check, workspace_role_check, admin_role_check or mutation_role_check: account admin, notifications, workspaces, workspace config, workspace notifications, ai_core and ingestion) use the auth way, because they pass plain legacy role values.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text: msflib-authz has no settings of its own. It reads the default tenant through the tenancy settings you pass as tenancy_settings (settings.scope("TENANCY")).

docs.title: Three questions about a role
docs.text:
Every row in role_assignment says "this principal holds this role, here". Three separate things decide what that means, and each lives in a different place.

Question Answered by Stored on What level of authority does the role grant? the role's tier: platform, tenant or workspace Role.tier Who defined the role, and who may use it? the role's owner: nobody (shared), a tenant, or a workspace Role.tenant_id, Role.workspace_id Where does this one grant apply? the assignment's scope RoleAssignment.tenant_id, RoleAssignment.workspace_id

Role.tenant_id is the owner, not the scope

The tenant_id and workspace_id columns on Role say where the role is defined. They never say where the role applies. A role's authority is decided by its tier together with each assignment's own tenant_id and workspace_id. The columns on the two tables share names, but they are different facts.

The columns are deliberately not named owner_tenant_id / owner_workspace_id: the longer name adds noise without removing the need to read this section. Whenever you see role_tenant_id / role_workspace_id in the code (for example in validation.py), it is the owner; assignment_tenant_id / assignment_workspace_id is the scope of a grant.

docs.title: Tier
docs.text:
The tier fixes what shape of scope an assignment must have, and how far the role reaches.

Tier Assignment tenant_id Assignment workspace_id Reaches platform NULL NULL everywhere tenant set NULL that tenant (and, for cascading permissions, its workspaces) workspace set set exactly that workspace

Consequences:

  • A tenant or platform role cannot be assigned "at a workspace". Giving a tenant-tier role a workspace_id is invalid, and so is giving a workspace-tier role no workspace_id. Only workspace-tier roles are assigned to a workspace. A tenant-tier role reaches workspaces through the tenant cascade, not through a workspace assignment.
  • A platform role must be assigned with both ids NULL. NULL ids are not what makes a role platform-wide: the role's tier does. NULL ids on an assignment of a tenant or workspace role are simply invalid, and such a row grants nothing.
  • A workspace_id always requires a tenant_id; a workspace belongs to a tenant.

docs.title: Owner
docs.text:
The owner restricts who may be granted the role. NULL means "no restriction".

Role owner (tenant_id, workspace_id) Meaning May be assigned (NULL, NULL) shared definition in any tenant or workspace its tier allows (T, NULL) defined by tenant T only inside tenant T (T, W) defined by workspace W of tenant T only inside workspace W

The seeded owner, admin, member and guest workspace roles are shared (NULL, NULL): one definition, assigned per workspace, with every assignment naming its own tenant and workspace. The seeded tenant roles (admin, user) are owned by the default tenant.

A tier and an owner are independent. A workspace-tier role can be shared, owned by a tenant (a per-tenant template) or owned by one workspace. A platform-tier role must have no owner. A tenant-tier role cannot be owned by a workspace.

docs.title: Assignment scope
docs.text: RoleAssignment.tenant_id / workspace_id say where this grant applies, for example "Ada is an admin in tenant 5", or "Grace is a member of workspace 12 in tenant 5". Which ids are required follows from the tier (above), and the ids must lie inside the role's owner (above).

docs.title: Valid and invalid combinations
docs.text:
An assignment is effective, meaning it can grant authority, only if all three of the following hold. This single rule is is_effective_assignment in validation.py; every resolution path uses it.

  1. Its scope has the shape its role's tier requires (the table under Tier).
  2. It lies inside the role's owner. For each of tenant and workspace: if the role has an owner there, the assignment must name exactly that id; if the role has none, any id is fine.
  3. It has not expired (expires_at is NULL or in the future).

The owner check only compares when the role has an owner, because a NULL owner means "shared". That asymmetry is intentional, and it does not leave the assignment's own NULLs unchecked:

  • If the role has an owner, a NULL assignment id fails the comparison (NULL is not equal to 5).
  • If the role is shared, a NULL assignment id is caught by the tier-shape check in step 1.

The two checks together cover every case:

Role (tier; owner) Assignment (tenant, workspace) Effective? Why platform; (NULL, NULL) (NULL, NULL) yes platform; (NULL, NULL) (5, NULL) no shape: platform needs no ids tenant; (NULL, NULL) shared (5, NULL) yes shared, tenant named tenant; (NULL, NULL) shared (NULL, NULL) no shape: tenant tier needs a tenant tenant; (5, NULL) (5, NULL) yes tenant; (5, NULL) (6, NULL) no owner: role is tenant 5's tenant; (5, NULL) (5, 3) no shape: tenant tier has no workspace workspace; (NULL, NULL) template (5, 3) yes workspace; (NULL, NULL) template (5, NULL) no shape: workspace tier needs a workspace workspace; (5, NULL) (5, 3) yes any workspace of tenant 5 workspace; (5, NULL) (6, 3) no owner: role is tenant 5's workspace; (5, 3) (5, 3) yes workspace; (5, 3) (5, 4) no owner: role is workspace 3's workspace; (5, 3) (NULL, NULL) no shape and owner

RoleService.grant rejects an invalid assignment with ValueError. Resolution also ignores one, so a row that was written some other way (a raw action, a data migration, a bug) still grants nothing. The database enforces what it can without joining tables:

  • ck_role_tier_scope on role: platform roles have no owner; tenant roles have no workspace owner; a workspace owner implies a tenant owner.
  • ck_role_assignment_scope on role_assignment: a workspace_id requires a tenant_id.
  • ck_role_assignment_source on role_assignment: source is runtime or legacy_backfill.
  • ck_role_scope_ids_positive and ck_role_assignment_ids_positive: scope ids, when set, are positive. The unique identity indexes treat NULL scope columns as equal by coalescing them to -1, so a real id must never equal the sentinel; RoleService also rejects non-positive ids with ValueError.

The tier-versus-assignment rule (step 1) and the owner rule (step 2) compare columns on two tables, which a CHECK constraint cannot do. They are enforced by the service on write and by resolution on read.

docs.title: How a permission is resolved
docs.text:
RoleService.has_permission(session, account_id=..., tenant_id=..., workspace_id=None, permission_key=...) loads the account's effective assignments for that scope, including those made to a group the account belongs to, and then applies the reach of each tier:

  • platform: always applies.
  • tenant: applies when the assignment's tenant is the request's tenant, and either the request is tenant-level (no workspace) or the permission was registered with tenant_cascade=True.
  • workspace: applies only when the assignment's (tenant_id, workspace_id) is exactly the request's pair. There is no cascade.

The permission is granted when any matching role bundles the key (or a prefix.* key covering it). platform_only=True considers platform-tier roles only.

docs.title: Role keys
docs.text:
get_role_keys_for(session, principal_kind=..., principal_id=..., tenant_id=None, workspace_id=None) returns the keys of the roles in effect at a scope, as RoleKey(tier, key) values. The tier is part of the value because the same string can exist at several tiers: the seeded admin is a tenant role and a workspace role. Without the tier, a workspace admin could be mistaken for a tenant admin.

  • Platform roles are always included.
  • Tenant roles are included for tenant_id.
  • Workspace roles are included for exactly (tenant_id, workspace_id).
  • With tenant_id=None, only platform roles are returned.

docs.title: Legacy roles
docs.text:
Account.role (root, admin, user) and User.type (owner, admin, member, guest) are read by the auth guards. The authz guards ignore them: only assignments and their bundled permissions count.

To move a route from RoleCheck to require_role without losing access, mirror the attributes into assignments first with the backfills (see Seeding). They write legacy_backfill assignments; a runtime grant is a separate row. The two sources are independent afterwards: revoking an assignment does not change the attribute, and editing the attribute does not change assignments until the backfill runs again.

The seeded role keys reuse the legacy values so the backfills mirror existing data. The shared names are safe because they live at different tiers and every authz check is tier-aware: a legacy admin becomes a tenant-tier admin, root a platform-tier root.

docs.title: Writing roles
docs.text:
Write through RoleService; the actions are plain data access.

  • create_role, ensure_role (get-or-create), add_permissions, grant, ensure_assignment (get-or-grant), revoke. The values the server decides are separate parameters, not schema fields: owner=RoleOwner(...) (default SHARED), is_system and created_by_account_id for a role; scope=RoleAssignmentScope(...) (default UNSCOPED) and granted_by_account_id for an assignment. Renewing an expired grant keeps its original grantor unless a new one is passed. The ensure_* methods are safe to repeat and to run from several processes at once: a caller that loses a creation race gets the winner's row.
  • Each public method is one closed unit of work: its writes run in savepoints and it commits once at the end, so a failure leaves nothing half-written. The batch methods (ensure_roles, bundle_permissions, sync_legacy_assignments, used by the seeders) commit once for the whole batch. Events fire on that commit. Because the commit is the session's, any other pending work in the same session is committed with it.
  • grant validates the assignment (tier shape, owner scope, expires_at in the future) and rejects an existing one with AssignmentExistsError; create_role raises RoleExistsError for a duplicate. Both are ValueError subclasses, and they are raised the same way when a concurrent writer wins the race, so callers handle one error rather than a raw IntegrityError.
  • Granting over an expired runtime assignment renews it (new expires_at; the original granter is kept unless granted_by_account_id is given) instead of failing, so an expired grant never blocks re-granting. A mirrored legacy assignment of the same role is a separate row and is left alone.
  • key, name and principal_id are trimmed, must not be blank, and keys and principal ids are limited to 255 characters; scope ids must be positive.
  • Events: see Events.

A row written straight through an action is not validated, but resolution ignores it if it breaks the rules above.

docs.title: Groups
docs.text:
A group is a set of accounts that can hold role assignments together. Assign a role to a group with principal_kind=PrincipalKind.group and the group's id as principal_id; every account that is a member then holds it, in addition to its own assignments. This applies when the principal is a user (an account); a group is not a member of another group. Resolution nests the account's memberships as a subquery, so the query size does not grow with the number of groups.

Visibility Who manages membership Who gets the group's roles workspace not restricted by the service; your route guard decides every member personal only the group's owner every member

A group belongs to a workspace, or to the workspace-agnostic bucket when its workspace_id is None (a real scope of its own, not "unscoped"). GroupService adds and removes members. Each call is one unit of work, like RoleService:

from msflib.authz.models import GroupMemberCreate
from msflib.authz.services import GroupService

service = GroupService()
service.add_member(
    session,
    data=GroupMemberCreate(account_id=42),
    group_id=group.id,
    added_by_account_id=current_account.id,
)
service.remove_member(session, id=member.id, removed_by_account_id=current_account.id)

group_id and the acting account come from the request, so they are service parameters, not fields of GroupMemberCreate. For a personal group the acting account must be the owner, otherwise ValueError. Adding an account that is already a member raises GroupMemberExistsError, also when two requests race. GroupCreate likewise has no workspace_id or owner_account_id; pass them with create(update={...}).

docs.title: Resource access
docs.text:
A resource access row gives one user or group a level on one resource, for example a file. Roles answer "what may this account do here"; access rows answer "what may this account do to this one thing". They are independent: AccessService never reads roles. The word permission in this module always means a permission key such as docs.publish; a level on a resource is an access level.

Level Meaning none explicit exclusion; blocks access inherited from a parent viewer read commenter read and comment editor read, comment and edit manager everything, including sharing

Resolution walks the resource and then its ancestors, nearest first. At the first level that has an access row for the account (directly, or through a group it belongs to) the highest matching level wins, none included, and farther ancestors are not consulted. No match gives None. The resource's owner is always manager. Use the can_read, can_comment, can_edit and can_manage helpers to turn a level into a yes or no.

from msflib.authz.models import AccessLevel, PrincipalKind, ResourceAccessCreate
from msflib.authz.services.access import AccessService, can_edit

service = AccessService()
service.grant(
    session,
    data=ResourceAccessCreate(
        principal_kind=PrincipalKind.user,
        principal_id="42",
        level=AccessLevel.editor,
    ),
    resource_type="drivelink_node",
    resource_id=12,
    workspace_id=7,
    granted_by_account_id=current_account.id,
)
level = service.resolve_access(
    session,
    resource_type="drivelink_node",
    resource_id=12,
    workspace_id=7,
    account_id=42,
    is_owner=False,
    ancestor_ids=[3, 1],
)
assert can_edit(level)

principal_id must be the user's account id or the group id as a positive integer without leading zeros ("42", not "042"); anything else raises a validation error, because resolution compares it as a string and such a row could never match. The resource (resource_type, resource_id), its workspace_id (None is the workspace-agnostic bucket, a real scope of its own) and the acting account come from the request, so they are parameters of grant, not fields of ResourceAccessCreate, which holds only the principal and the level. resource_type is 1 to 64 characters and resource_id positive, otherwise ValueError. Granting again to the same principal updates the level, records the new grantor when one is passed (otherwise the original stays), and keeps the original workspace_id. revoke deletes an access row. resolve_access and resolve_accesses take the resource's workspace_id and count only rows granted in exactly that workspace (None matches only the workspace-agnostic bucket, not every workspace), so a grant in workspace 7 never authorizes the same resource id in workspace 8. For lists, resolve_accesses resolves many resources at once: one query for the account's groups and one access query per 500 distinct resource ids (a single batch for most lists).

docs.title: Events
docs.text:
RoleService emits two events, role-assignment-granted and role-assignment-revoked, with RoleAssignmentEventName.ROLE_ASSIGNMENT_GRANTED and RoleAssignmentEventName.ROLE_ASSIGNMENT_REVOKED. GroupService emits group-member-added and group-member-removed, named GroupMemberEventName.GROUP_MEMBER_ADDED and GroupMemberEventName.GROUP_MEMBER_REMOVED. AccessService emits resource-access-granted and resource-access-revoked, named ResourceAccessEventName.RESOURCE_ACCESS_GRANTED and ResourceAccessEventName.RESOURCE_ACCESS_REVOKED. Import the names and the payload contracts from the package's eventbus.

from msflib.authz.eventbus import EVENT_CONTRACTS, RoleAssignmentEventName
from msflib.eventbus import get_emitter

def on_granted(row, payload): ...

get_emitter().on(RoleAssignmentEventName.ROLE_ASSIGNMENT_GRANTED, on_granted)
  • When. After the outermost commit of the unit of work, never before. A rollback discards them. A listener error is logged, not raised, so it cannot undo the write.
  • Arguments. row is a snapshot of the written row's columns, taken before the commit: for a role assignment id, role_id, principal_kind, principal_id, tenant_id, workspace_id, source and so on; for a group member group_id and account_id; for resource access resource_type, resource_id, principal_kind, principal_id, level, workspace_id and so on. It stays readable after the session is closed, so a listener may run later or on another thread. It is not the ORM instance. For revoked it is the row as it was before it was deleted.
  • payload. For role assignments: principal_kind, principal_id, role_key, tenant_id, workspace_id; role_key is left out when the role row no longer exists. For group members: group_id, account_id and, on added, added_by_account_id. For resource access: resource_type, resource_id, principal_kind and principal_id; granted adds level (its name, such as viewer) and workspace_id.

docs.title: Grant a workspace role and check it
docs.text:
A shared editor template (tier workspace, no owner), granted to account 42 in workspace 7 of the default tenant:

from msflib.authz import PERMISSION_REGISTRY, PrincipalKind, RoleService, RoleTier
from msflib.authz.models import RoleAssignmentScope, RoleAssignmentCreate, RoleCreate

PERMISSION_REGISTRY.register("docs.publish")
service = RoleService()

editor = service.ensure_role(
    session, data=RoleCreate(key="editor", name="Editor", tier=RoleTier.workspace)
)
service.add_permissions(session, role_id=editor.id, permission_keys=["docs.publish"])
service.grant(
    session,
    data=RoleAssignmentCreate(
        role_id=editor.id, principal_kind=PrincipalKind.user, principal_id="42"
    ),
    scope=RoleAssignmentScope(tenant_id=tenant_id, workspace_id=7),
)

service.has_permission(
    session, account_id=42, tenant_id=tenant_id, workspace_id=7, permission_key="docs.publish"
)  # True
service.has_permission(
    session, account_id=42, tenant_id=tenant_id, workspace_id=8, permission_key="docs.publish"
)  # False: workspace roles do not reach other workspaces

RoleCreate and RoleAssignmentCreate hold only what a client may send. The values the server decides are separate parameters: owner=RoleOwner(...) (default SHARED) for a role, scope=RoleAssignmentScope(...) (default UNSCOPED) for an assignment, and granted_by_account_id / created_by_account_id for the actor. Build them in the endpoint from the request context; never read them from the body.

Granting the same role without workspace_id raises ValueError ("tier=workspace requires both tenant_id and workspace_id set"), because a workspace-tier role needs a workspace.

docs.title: Guard a route with a permission
docs.text:
A document-publishing feature, end to end. The module owns the key; the host app seeds and grants.

from fastapi import Depends
from msflib.authz import PERMISSION_REGISTRY, PrincipalKind, RoleService, RoleTier
from msflib.authz.models import RoleAssignmentScope, RoleAssignmentCreate, RoleCreate
from msflib.authz.seed import seed_role_permissions, seed_system_roles

# 1. The feature registers its key at import time (not in a function).
PERMISSION_REGISTRY.register("docs.publish")  # workspace-level only: no tenant cascade

# 2. At startup, after every module is imported: seed roles and bundle keys.
roles = seed_system_roles(session, default_tenant_id=tenant_id)
seed_role_permissions(session, roles=roles)  # the seeded workspace owner and admin get docs.publish

# 3. Optionally, a custom workspace role that can publish and nothing else.
service = RoleService()
editor = service.ensure_role(
    session, data=RoleCreate(key="editor", name="Editor", tier=RoleTier.workspace)
)
service.add_permissions(session, role_id=editor.id, permission_keys=["docs.publish"])

# 4. Grant it to account 42 in workspace 7.
service.grant(
    session,
    data=RoleAssignmentCreate(
        role_id=editor.id, principal_kind=PrincipalKind.user, principal_id="42"
    ),
    scope=RoleAssignmentScope(tenant_id=tenant_id, workspace_id=7),
)

# 5. Guard the route (authz comes from get_authz_dependencies, see above).
@router.post("/{workspace_slug}/docs/{doc_id}/publish")
def publish(doc_id: int, _: bool = Depends(authz.require_permission("docs.publish"))): ...

What happens for account 42:

Request Result Why publish in workspace 7 allowed editor is held in exactly that workspace and bundles docs.publish publish in workspace 8 403 a workspace role does not reach other workspaces a tenant-tier admin publishes in workspace 7 403 docs.publish is not tenant_cascade; hold a workspace role, or register the key with tenant_cascade=True the seeded workspace owner publishes in workspace 7 allowed seed_role_permissions bundled the key into owner

The same key also reads naturally in code: service.has_permission(session, account_id=42, tenant_id=tenant_id, workspace_id=7, permission_key="docs.publish") returns True for the first row.

For a tenant-wide action, register the key with tenant_cascade=True if tenant admins should reach it in every workspace, and guard with tier="tenant":

PERMISSION_REGISTRY.register("docs.audit", tenant_cascade=True)

@router.get("/audit", dependencies=[Depends(authz.require_permission("docs.audit", tier="tenant"))])
def audit(): ...

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• A role is assigned but grants nothing. The assignment is not effective. Check, in order, that its tenant_id / workspace_id match the role's tier (platform: none; tenant: tenant only; workspace: both), that they lie inside the role's owner, and that expires_at has not passed. Rows written through a raw action are not validated, and resolution silently ignores a bad one.
  • ValueError from grant. The message names the rule that failed: tier shape, owner scope, a missing role, an expires_at that is not in the future, or an existing unexpired assignment (AssignmentExistsError).
  • Two processes seeded at once. Seeding and the backfills use ensure_role / ensure_assignment, so concurrent startups converge on the same rows instead of failing on the unique index.
  • A workspace admin does not pass require_role(RoleKey(RoleTier.tenant, "admin")). Intended. The tier is part of the key; ask for the workspace-tier key, or use require_permission.
  • A tenant admin cannot act in a workspace. Tenant roles reach workspaces only for permissions registered with tenant_cascade=True. Otherwise grant a workspace-tier role in that workspace.
  • A new permission is missing from root or admin. seed_role_permissions bundles the keys registered when it runs. Run it after every module has been imported.
  • A role's key, tier or owner cannot be changed. They are immutable because changing them would reinterpret existing assignments. Create a new role and move the assignments.
  • Revoking an assignment did not remove access to an auth route. RoleCheck and WorkspaceRoleCheck read the attribute, not assignments. Authz guards honour the revoke.
  • Requests are denied with no tenant. get_current_tenant is wired but returned nothing. A missing request tenant is denied, never defaulted.
  • A backfill removed assignments it should not have. It treats its input as the complete set. Pass every account or membership.

docs.text: See the generated msflib.authz reference.

docs.text:

  • tenancy: the Tenant model and the default-tenant resolver the guards fall back to.
  • workspaces: workspaces and membership, the source of workspace-tier roles.
  • Scopes, tenancy and workspaces: the scope dimensions in general.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
msflib-conversation is a chat-style conversation layer for host apps: channels, direct messages, threads, messages, membership, reactions, pins, read state and attached resources, with access control built in. It is also the identity substrate for the AI modules: a conversation's public_id is the conversation_id scope dimension that ai-core checkpoints and memory, and knowledge scoping, key off, and a thread's public_id is the sub_thread_id.

It has no UI or realtime transport. It gives you the tables, services, an optional HTTP router, and an optional bridge that lets an ai-api agent write its turns into a conversation.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
[tool.poetry.dependencies]
msflib = { git = "https://github.com/msflib/fastapi.git", subdirectory = "core", rev = "core-v0.2.1" }
msflib-conversation = { git = "https://github.com/msflib/fastapi.git", subdirectory = "modules/conversation", rev = "conversation-v0.2.0" }

Dependencies are msflib, msflib-tenancy and python-ulid. There are no extras. The module does not import account, workspaces, ai_core or ai_api at module scope: it takes your account and workspace objects through small protocols that only need an id.

msflib.conversation lazily exports the settings, actions, contracts, services, errors and policy functions (ConversationScope, Participant, ChannelService, AccessService, can_read, ...). Models and schemas are in msflib.conversation.models, and the router and deps are imported from their submodules.

docs.title: Wiring into a host app
docs.text:
1. Add ConversationSettings to your settings class.
  2. Import msflib.conversation.models so the tables are created (and migrated).
  3. Mount the router, passing your own session, account, workspace and tenant dependencies.
from msflib.conversation.router import router as create_conversation_router

app.include_router(
    create_conversation_router(
        get_session=get_session,
        get_current_account=get_current_account,
        get_current_workspace=get_current_workspace,   # optional
        get_current_tenant=get_current_tenant,         # optional
        settings=settings,
        prefix="/conversation",
        tags=["conversation"],
    )
)

get_current_account only needs to return an object with an id. Without a workspace dependency, every request is in the workspace-less bucket (workspace_id=None). Without a tenant dependency, the tenant with the slug from your TENANCY.DEFAULT_TENANT_SLUG setting (default unless you changed it) is looked up in the database and must be seeded, otherwise requests fail with 500.

The router has no prefix of its own (prefix="" by default); its paths are:

Path Methods /conversations POST create (channel, dm, group dm or personal; for dms, participants lists the other people), GET list /conversations/{public_id} GET, PATCH /conversations/{public_id}/archive, /unarchive POST /conversations/{public_id}/members POST join yourself (public channels) or invite someone else /conversations/{public_id}/members/{member_id} DELETE remove or leave, PATCH change role /conversations/{public_id}/messages GET history (keyset paged), POST post /conversations/{public_id}/read PUT mark read /conversations/{public_id}/pinned GET /conversations/{public_id}/resources GET, POST link a resource /messages/{message_id} PATCH edit, DELETE /messages/{message_id}/thread POST reply in a thread /messages/{message_id}/reactions/{emoji} PUT, DELETE /messages/{message_id}/pin POST, DELETE /threads/{thread_public_id}/messages GET

Access checks (does the conversation exist, is the caller allowed to see it) run once in the dependency layer, not in each endpoint. To override them, build a namespace with get_conversation_dependencies(...) from msflib.conversation.deps, replace the attributes you need, and pass it as dependencies= to the router. Its members are require_account, get_participant, get_conversation_scope, get_conversation_context, get_message_context, get_thread_context and access_service. A conversation that does not exist in the caller's scope returns 404, and one the caller may not read returns 403. Without get_current_tenant, the default tenant is looked up with the slug from tenancy_settings= (the root settings or their TENANCY scope) when you build the namespace; omit it and the slug default is used.

See Mounting routes for the general router pattern.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Settings live in the CONVERSATION namespace, and the field names are lowercase.

Key Default Notes default_visibility private Visibility for channels created without one: public, private or personal. max_message_chars 8000 Longer messages and edits are rejected. history_page_size 50 Default page size for history reads. history_page_size_max 200 Upper bound on a requested page size. edit_window_minutes 0 Minutes after posting during which a message can be edited; 0 means unlimited. allow_guest_posting False Whether members with the guest role may post. allow_private_to_public False Whether a private conversation's visibility may be changed to public. retention_days None Declared, currently has no effect (#278). Not read by any code in the module. purge_soft_deleted_after_days 30 Declared, currently has no effect (#278). Not read by any code in the module, and no code emits the purge event conversation-messages-purged.

Known issue (#277)

Because the fields are lowercase and environment matching is case-sensitive, CONVERSATION__MAX_MESSAGE_CHARS does not set anything. Use the flat aliases instead, which work whether your settings nest the namespace or mix it in: CONVERSATION_DEFAULT_VISIBILITY, CONVERSATION_MAX_MESSAGE_CHARS, CONVERSATION_HISTORY_PAGE_SIZE, CONVERSATION_HISTORY_PAGE_SIZE_MAX, CONVERSATION_EDIT_WINDOW_MINUTES, CONVERSATION_ALLOW_GUEST_POSTING, CONVERSATION_ALLOW_PRIVATE_TO_PUBLIC, CONVERSATION_RETENTION_DAYS and CONVERSATION_PURGE_SOFT_DELETED_AFTER_DAYS. With a nested CONVERSATION object, CONVERSATION__max_message_chars (lowercase field name) also works.

docs.title: Key concepts
docs.text:
Conversation. The container. kind is channel, dm, group_dm or personal, and visibility is public, private or personal; the two axes are independent. public_id (a conv_-prefixed ULID) is the only identifier exposed outside the module and is what URLs and AI scopes use. Direct conversations are get-or-create keyed on their member set, so starting a dm with the same people returns the same conversation.

Thread. A first-class sub-conversation anchored to a root message, with its own thrd_-prefixed public_id. Replying in a thread through POST /messages/{id}/thread creates the thread on the first reply.

Message. Posted into a conversation or thread by a user, an agent or the system. Deletion is a soft delete (a tombstone). History is keyset-paginated on the message id: before_id and after_id rather than offsets. Content may carry blocks and a client-supplied client_msg_id. @mentions in the content are extracted when the message is posted.

Member and participant. Membership rows are polymorphic: (member_kind, member_id) with kind user or agent, a role (owner, admin, member, guest) and a status (invited, active, left, removed). Read state (last read message, notification level, mute and star) lives on the same row. A Participant(kind, id, tenant_id) is the caller projected into that shape; id is a string, so account ids are stringified.

Scope. ConversationScope(tenant_id, workspace_id, conversation_id, sub_thread_id) is the typed scope the services and actions take. workspace_id=None is the explicit workspace-less bucket. AccessService.resolve_conversation(session, scope=..., participant=...) is the single entry point that turns a caller-supplied conversation_id string into a verified row (exists, same tenant and workspace, caller allowed to read it) and returns it with the caller's membership. Anything downstream, such as a checkpointer config or a knowledge scope, should be built from a conversation resolved this way.

Policy. can_read, can_post, can_manage and can_change_visibility are pure functions over loaded rows. Who may join a public channel or be invited is delegated to a MemberEligibility object; the default, SameTenantEligibility, allows anyone in the conversation's tenant. Pass your own to AccessService(eligibility=...) to tie eligibility to, for example, workspace membership.

Services. Each service is a class taking its actions and settings at construction: ChannelService, MembershipService, MessagingService, ThreadService, HistoryService, ReadStateService, ReactionService and ResourceService. Channel and membership calls are closed units of work: each commits itself, writes a timeline system_event message for the change, and emits its domain event after commit.

Resources. A ResourceLink attaches an external thing (resource_kind plus resource_ref) to a conversation or message. Kinds are validated against RESOURCE_KIND_REGISTRY, which starts with document, url and image; add your own with RESOURCE_KIND_REGISTRY.register("note") at startup.

Events. Register listeners on the app emitter: app_emitter = bind_app_emitter(app) at app creation, then @app_emitter.on("conversation-message-posted"). Listeners fire for events emitted from the router. When you call the services yourself, for example ChannelService().create_channel(...) in a script, the app emitter is not active and nothing reaches app-bound listeners; wrap that code in with use_app_emitter(app): (both from msflib.eventbus). Domain events such as conversation-created, conversation-message-posted, conversation-member-joined and conversation-thread-started carry the conversation's public_id and scope values, never the integer primary key (messages are addressed by integer id). Row-level lifecycle events come from ModelAction. See Event bus.

docs.title: Channels, messages and history with the services
docs.text:
This runs as written against in-memory SQLite. It seeds tenant 1 first: SQLite does not enforce the tenant_id foreign key, but Postgres does.

import msflib.conversation.models  # noqa: F401  (registers the tables)
from msflib.conversation.contracts import ConversationScope, Participant
from msflib.conversation.models import ConversationCreate, MessageCreate
from msflib.conversation.models.enums import MemberKind
from msflib.conversation.services import (
    AccessService,
    ChannelService,
    HistoryService,
    MessagingService,
)
from msflib.tenancy.models.tenant import Tenant  # noqa: F401
from msflib.tenancy.resolver import resolve_default_tenant_id
from sqlalchemy.pool import StaticPool
from sqlmodel import Session, SQLModel, create_engine

engine = create_engine("sqlite://", connect_args={"check_same_thread": False}, poolclass=StaticPool)
SQLModel.metadata.create_all(engine)
with Session(engine) as session:
    resolve_default_tenant_id(session)     # seeds tenant 1
    session.commit()

owner = Participant(kind=MemberKind.user, id="u1", tenant_id=1)
scope = ConversationScope(tenant_id=1, workspace_id=7)

with Session(engine) as session:
    conversation, membership = ChannelService().create_channel(
        session,
        scope=scope,
        data=ConversationCreate(name="general", slug="general"),
        created_by=owner,
    )
    print(conversation.kind, conversation.visibility, membership.role)   # channel private owner

    resolved, member = AccessService().resolve_conversation(
        session,
        scope=ConversationScope(
            tenant_id=1, workspace_id=7, conversation_id=conversation.public_id
        ),
        participant=owner,
    )
    MessagingService().post_message(
        session,
        conversation=resolved,
        sender=owner,
        actor_membership=member,
        data=MessageCreate(content="hello @team"),
    )
    page = HistoryService().list_conversation_history(session, conversation=resolved)
    print([(m.content, m.sender_kind) for m in page])                     # [('hello @team', 'user')]

create_channel returns the conversation with the creator's owner membership. post_message raises PermissionError if the membership may not post and ValueError for empty or too-long content. Services use ConversationSettings() defaults unless you pass conversation_settings= at construction. In your own code pass conversation_settings=settings.scope("CONVERSATION").unwrap(), or host overrides are ignored: the router applies them, but a bare MessagingService().post_message(...) does not.

docs.title: Through HTTP
docs.text:
With the router mounted at /conversation and a seeded default tenant:

from fastapi.testclient import TestClient

client = TestClient(app)
created = client.post("/conversation/conversations", json={"name": "general", "slug": "general"})
public_id = created.json()["public_id"]                       # 201, "conv_..."
client.post(f"/conversation/conversations/{public_id}/messages", json={"content": "hello"})
client.get(f"/conversation/conversations/{public_id}/messages").json()   # newest first

Request bodies are the module's own ConversationCreate, MessageCreate, MemberAddRequest, ResourceLinkCreate and so on. Tenant, workspace and the acting user always come from your dependencies, never from the body.

docs.title: Persisting AI agent turns
docs.text:
msflib.conversation.integrations.ai_bridge wires an ai-api agent to a conversation without either module importing the other. The user's question and the agent's reply are written as ordinary messages (sender_kind user and agent), so the conversation is the readable transcript, separate from the LangGraph checkpoint state. This is how the repository's reference site mounts it:

from fastapi import Depends
from msflib.ai_api.router import router as create_ai_router
from msflib.conversation.integrations import ai_bridge

app.include_router(
    create_ai_router(
        settings=settings,
        get_session=get_session,
        get_current_account=get_current_account,
        get_current_workspace=get_current_workspace,
        get_current_tenant=get_current_tenant,
        transcript_writer_factory=ai_bridge.build_transcript_writer_factory(
            lambda: Session(engine), agent_id="assistant"
        ),
        speaker_label_factory=ai_bridge.build_speaker_label_factory(resolve_display_name),
        prefix="/ai",
    ),
    dependencies=[
        Depends(
            ai_bridge.build_conversation_access_dependency(
                get_session,
                get_current_account,
                get_current_workspace=get_current_workspace,
                get_current_tenant=get_current_tenant,
            )
        )
    ],
)

build_conversation_access_dependency reads conversation_id (and sub_thread_id) from the request body and rejects callers who cannot read that conversation before the agent touches any checkpoint or memory state; requests without a conversation_id pass through. build_transcript_writer_factory returns a factory ai-api calls per request; it opens a short session per write, adds the agent as a member of the conversation if it is not an active member, and returns None when the request has no conversation_id. build_speaker_label_factory prefixes each user message with the sender's name and id so an agent in a multi-user conversation can tell people apart; resolve_display_name is your callable (account_id: str) -> str | None. This snippet was not run end to end because it needs a working LLM and a host account system; every name in it is checked against the source. engine and resolve_display_name are supplied by your host. Other helpers in the module are conversation_dimensions (the scope dimensions for a conversation and thread), add_agent_participant and register_memory_cleanup_listener.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Cause and fix 500 "Default tenant has not been seeded" The tenant dependency is missing and no tenant with the configured TENANCY.DEFAULT_TENANT_SLUG (default unless changed) exists. Pass get_current_tenant or run your startup seeding with the same settings. ValueError: A conversation with slug 'general' already exists on a fresh database Can be a missing tenant row: with foreign keys enforced the tenant failure is masked by this message. Seed the tenant. 404 for a conversation that exists AccessService matches tenant and workspace exactly, and workspace_id=None is its own bucket. Pass get_current_workspace consistently with how the conversation was created. 403 on a channel you can find by id The caller is not a member of a private conversation, or is not eligible under your MemberEligibility. CONVERSATION__MAX_MESSAGE_CHARS has no effect Field names are lowercase. Use CONVERSATION_MAX_MESSAGE_CHARS; see the Known issue notice under Configuration. PermissionError on post_message The membership is missing, not active, or a guest while allow_guest_posting is false. ValueError: Unregistered resource_kind Register it: RESOURCE_KIND_REGISTRY.register("your_kind"). ValueError: created_by.tenant_id must match scope.tenant_id The Participant and ConversationScope disagree on tenant. Build both from the same resolved tenant id. Retention settings do nothing retention_days and purge_soft_deleted_after_days are not implemented yet (#278), and no code emits conversation-messages-purged.
