docs.title: typed_router
docs.text: typed_router — inject runtime Pydantic/SQLModel validation types into FastAPI route handlers while keeping decorator-style ergonomics.

docs.title: Why this exists
docs.text:
FastAPI resolves request-body schemas by inspecting a function's __signature__, not its source-level __annotations__. That means we can replace a parameter's annotation with a concrete model class before APIRouter.add_api_route is called, and FastAPI will validate the incoming request against that class — while the function body still receives a plain argument under the same name.

This module wraps :class:~fastapi.APIRouter in a thin :class:EnhancedAPIRouter overlay that adds a validation_types keyword argument to every HTTP-method decorator. Only parameters listed in validation_types are affected; every other parameter annotation (including FastAPI Depends markers) is left untouched.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
::

from fastapi import APIRouter, Depends
from typing import Any
from sqlmodel import Session
from msflib.api import create_enhanced_router

api_router = APIRouter(prefix="/items")
enh_router = create_enhanced_router(api_router)

@enh_router.post(
    "/",
    response_model=ItemRead,
    status_code=201,
    validation_types={"data": ItemCreate},
)
def create_item(
    *,
    session: Session = Depends(get_session),
    data: Any,           # annotation is replaced at registration time
) -> Any:
    return item_action.create(session=session, data=data)

The underlying api_router is completely unmodified and should still be passed to app.include_router. EnhancedAPIRouter is a registration-time overlay only.

docs.title: ModuleSettingsBase
docs.text:
Bases: BaseModel

Base class for module settings.

Module settings classes should declare a namespace that matches the key used by SettingsBase.scope() (e.g. CORE).

flat_aliases maps simple, non-namespaced env var keys (e.g. ENABLE_SSO_AUTH) to the nested settings path (e.g. AUTH.ENABLE_SSO_AUTH). Use it whenever a deployment prefers flat env var names — whether for a new site with a simpler naming convention or when migrating from pre-namespace configurations. Nested keys (e.g. AUTH__ENABLE_SSO_AUTH) take precedence over flat aliases when both are set. Subclasses can override this mapping to provide their own aliases.

A host AppSettings can also override a module default at code level by declaring a root field with the same bare name (e.g. ENABLE_SSO_AUTH: bool = True on the host class). scope("AUTH").ENABLE_SSO_AUTH will then return the root field's value. This is intentional: the root field acts as a permanent code-level override of the module default.

request_override_allowlist (optional) is a set of configuration keys that are allowed to be overridden in per-request contexts via ScopedConfigService. If not set (None), all keys are allowed. Set it to a non-empty set to constrain which keys can be mutated via untrusted request paths (e.g., to prevent setting secrets or critical config). The service validates overrides against this allowlist before applying them.

If annotation is a plain mapping, define the policy model in sibling policy.py and follow naming convention from _policy_schema_candidate_names.

docs.title: SettingsBase(**data: Any)
docs.text:
Bases: BaseSettings

Base application settings.

Module settings composition uses two approaches:

Option A: Direct Mixin Inheritance relies on multiple inheritance and field overrides, which is simpler but may be susceptible to name clashes and uses normal Pydantic validation and .env support.

class Settings(ModuleASettings, ModuleBSettings, SettingsBase):
    ...
    OVERRIDDEN_SETTING_1 = "overridden_value"   # from module A
    OVERRIDDEN_SETTING_2 = "overridden_value"   # from module B
    ...

Option B: Composed Settings with Nested Modules relies on nested settings objects (e.g. AUTH) and also uses normal Pydantic validation and .env support.

class Settings(SettingsBase):
    MODULE_A: ModuleASettings = ModuleASettings(
        OVERRIDDEN_SETTING_1="overridden_value",
        ...
    )
    MODULE_B: ModuleBSettings = ModuleBSettings(
        OVERRIDDEN_SETTING_2="overridden_value",
        ...
    )

Consumer projects can override specific values by passing settings to the composed settings class (or by subclassing and overriding defaults).

Returns a flat dict of overrides.

If the module defines request_override_allowlist, ensure all override keys are in that set. Otherwise, all keys are allowed. If collect_errors is True, returns a list of (key, reason) tuples for rejected keys. Otherwise, raises ValueError listing all unsupported string keys and rejects non-string keys with ValueError.

The merge applies layers in this order: tenant -> workspace -> user -> request override

docs.title: errors
docs.text:
Shared error classification for ingestion-style background workers.

Generic -- no module-specific logic -- so any module's worker (documents, knowledge's extraction worker, ingestion's pipeline-stage wrapper, etc.) can reuse the same terminal-vs-retryable classification instead of each maintaining its own copy. Lives here rather than in any one consumer module so it can be shared without creating a dependency between them (e.g. msflib.ingestion deliberately doesn't depend on msflib.documents).

docs.title: is_importable(*module_names: str) -> bool cached
docs.text:
True if every named module can be imported (cached for this process).

A cheap availability probe for optional-dependency gating (is_available()-style checks). Returns False only when the named module itself (or a parent package of it) is missing. Other failures — a genuine bug in an installed module (e.g. a SyntaxError), or an ImportError from one of its dependencies rather than the module being probed — still propagate, since misreporting those as "not installed" would hide the real failure instead of surfacing it.

Pass multiple names when a feature needs more than one optional module present.

docs.title: readiness
docs.text:
Readiness: which deployment requirements are met, and which are not.

Checks answer "is this requirement met?" and never change anything. Remedies are the safe, idempotent fixes for checks. Each msflib module may ship <module>.readiness with a registry; :meth:Suite.from_settings collects the registries of the modules an application composes, adds core's own, and the application adds its own::

from msflib.core.readiness import Suite

suite = Suite.from_settings(settings, engine=engine, migration=MIGRATION,
                            unmanaged_tables=["langchain_pg_*"])

# python -m msflib.core.readiness --suite app.readiness:suite --profile prod --fix

docs.title: capture
docs.text:
Capture library logging and Python warnings while checks run.

Libraries such as Alembic log dozens of INFO lines and warn through logging and warnings. Printed as they happen they bury the report; captured, the warnings become findings attached to the check that caused them and the rest is dropped (or kept with --verbose).

Attribution follows the thread, not "whichever check is running now". A check runs on its own thread (so it can time out) and that thread carries a :class:_Token naming the check. Threads it starts inherit the token, so everything a check causes belongs to it, even when its thread outlives the timeout and the next check has already started. Whatever no check thread emitted is kept separately as unattributed.

The hooks that make this work are process-global (the root logging handlers, warnings and Thread.start), so one capture runs at a time. A thread that outlives its timeout is abandoned: its output is dropped, and the hooks stay in place until no abandoned thread is alive.

--fix may only apply a migration without a human when nothing in it can destroy data. A revision script is arbitrary Python, so this is a conservative scan of the revision file (not its downgrade()), not a proof: it flags what it recognises and anything it cannot read. A flagged revision is never applied automatically; the operator reviews it and runs the migration.

A read-only question about the deployment.

requires lists other check ids: when one of them failed, this check is reported as BLOCKED (one root cause) instead of failing again with its own copy of the same problem. paid marks a check that calls an external, billable service; --offline skips it. needs names the suite resources ("engine", "migration") the check cannot run without; when one is missing the check is skipped and the run warns that it was not verified. promote_warnings turns a PASS into a WARN when the check emitted warning-level log lines or Python warnings; switch it off for a check whose library is known to be noisy.

docs.title: reject_if_not_public_ip(address: str, *, hostname: str) -> None
docs.text:
Raise ValueError if address isn't a public, routable IP.

Shared SSRF-guarding primitive: any caller resolving a hostname before connecting to it (fetching a URL, validating a downstream-configured dictionary/data source, ...) should reject private/internal addresses rather than connecting to whatever a hostname happens to resolve to. See resolve_public_ips/validate_public_http_url below for the usual entry points -- this is the primitive they share.

docs.title: resolve_public_ips(hostname: str) -> list[str]
docs.text:
Resolve hostname and reject it if any address is non-public.

Guards against SSRF (fetching cloud metadata endpoints, internal services, loopback, etc.) via a caller-supplied hostname. A caller that opens the actual connection itself (rather than handing a URL to a library that does its own DNS resolution) should call this again at connect time, on the same lookup that opens the socket, rather than trusting an earlier, separate lookup -- otherwise a malicious DNS server can answer a public IP for an earlier check and a private one for the actual connection (DNS-rebinding TOCTOU). See msflib.ai_core.tools.fetch_url's connect-time transport for that pattern; validate_public_http_url below does only the early check.

docs.title: validate_public_http_url(url: str) -> str
docs.text:
Validate url is http(s) with a hostname resolving to a public address.

Returns url unchanged, for convenient call-site chaining (e.g. url = validate_public_http_url(url) across a redirect chain). This is the early, one-shot check -- it doesn't itself close the DNS-rebinding TOCTOU window described on resolve_public_ips; a caller that opens the connection itself should re-validate at connect time instead of relying on this alone.

docs.title: msflib.db
docs.text: Part of the msflib core package.

docs.title: cli
docs.text:
The initial_data entry point shared by downstream applications.

An application's initial_data.py only supplies what is its own (the engine, its :class:~msflib.db.migrations.MigrationConfig and a seed function)::

from msflib.db.cli import run_initial_data_cli

def main(argv=None) -> int:
    return run_initial_data_cli(
        engine=engine,
        config=MIGRATION,
        seed=seed_initial_data,
        environment=settings.ENVIRONMENT,
        argv=argv,
    )

if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())

python -m app.initial_data migrates the database (see :func:~msflib.db.migrations.migrate) and seeds it; it is safe to run on every start and never drops data. --reset drops everything first and is refused when environment is production or prod; on any non-local database it also needs --yes or an interactive confirmation (typing RESET; the seed CLI's classifier decides which databases count as non-local). --check only reports what would be done (state, pending revisions, drift) and changes nothing; exit code 0 means there is nothing to do, 3 means changes are pending.

Migrate (or with --reset, rebuild) the database and seed it. Returns an exit code.

docs.title: init_db(engine: Engine, metadata: MetaData, create_tables=False, seeder_config: SeederConfig | None = None) -> None
docs.text: Initializes the database by optionally creating tables and running seeders. This function should be called after all SQLModel models have been imported in the script to ensure metadata is correctly populated. Table creation is optional and intended for non-Alembic workflows (e.g., quick prototypes or testing). Args: engine (Engine): SQLAlchemy Engine instance connected to the target database. metadata (MetaData): SQLAlchemy MetaData containing table definitions. create_tables (bool, optional): If True, drops all existing tables and creates new ones based on the provided metadata. Defaults to False. seeder_config (SeederConfig, optional): Configuration for running the data seeding process. If provided, it will use the defined seeders and data paths to populate the database. Notes: - This drops every table in metadata when create_tables=True. For deployed apps use msflib.db.migrations.migrate (and msflib.db.cli.run_initial_data_cli), which never drop data; see the core README. - Alembic is recommended for managing schema migrations in production. - All models must be imported before calling this function to register them in metadata.

docs.title: limits
docs.text:
Limits the database enforces, shared by request schemas, services and actions.

Declare a limit once as a pydantic Annotated type and use it on both the table column and the Create/Update field: SQLModel reads max_length from Field into the column's VARCHAR(n) and pydantic raises a validation error for an oversized value, which FastAPI answers with a 422 where a bare database error would surface as a 500. SQLite ignores most of these limits, so a test on SQLite alone never notices a missing one::

ResourceType = Annotated[str, NON_BLANK_TEXT, Field(max_length=64)]

Declare the alias with a literal Annotated so type checkers can read it; a type built by a function call is not a valid annotation for them.

Name an alias after the concept, not the length: ExternalId, not Text255. Values that arrive as service arguments rather than through a schema (a string from a query parameter or an environment variable) go through msflib.core.typing.coerce first, then the same limits apply.

Smallest and largest value an integer column of column_type holds.

None when column_type is not an integer type. SQLite stores every integer column as a signed 64-bit value, so only 64 bits count there.

docs.title: migrations
docs.text:
Bring a database to the current schema, whatever state it is in.

Deploy scripts should not have to know whether a database is new, tracked by Alembic, or older than Alembic tracking. :func:migrate inspects it and picks:

  • empty database: create_all and stamp Alembic at head. A historic migration chain rarely builds a schema from nothing, and does not need to. The catch: create_all only knows the tables in the metadata, so migration-only operations (data inserts, views, triggers, functions) are not applied to a new database. If your chain has such steps, set MigrationConfig.fresh_database="upgrade" to run the whole chain on an empty database instead.
  • Alembic-tracked database: alembic upgrade head.
  • tables but no version row (kept in sync with create_all so far): stamp baseline_revision, then upgrade head. Migrations after the baseline should tolerate tables and columns that create_all already added (see the README for the pattern).
  • SQLite (development and tests): create_all, no Alembic.
  • no Alembic revisions yet (an app that has not generated its first migration): create_all, which creates missing tables but never alters existing ones. Nothing is dropped.

Two separate guarantees:

  • Atomic (PostgreSQL and SQLite): every path runs in one transaction (on SQLite an explicit one is begun), so a failure leaves the database unchanged. This relies on transactional DDL. On a database whose DDL commits implicitly (MySQL, MariaDB) earlier statements stay when a later one fails, so a failed migration can leave it partly migrated: back up first and rehearse.

A revision that needs a statement PostgreSQL cannot run in a transaction (CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, ALTER TYPE ... ADD VALUE on old servers) therefore cannot run through :func:migrate: PostgreSQL refuses it, or Alembic raises (autocommit_block()), the whole migration rolls back and nothing is committed. Write such a revision with with op.get_context().autocommit_block(): around the statement (a bare statement fails under the standalone command too, which also runs inside a transaction), apply it on its own with alembic upgrade, then run :func:migrate. - Serialized (PostgreSQL only): the transaction holds a Postgres advisory lock, so concurrent starts (several containers or workers) take turns. Other databases are not locked; run one start at a time there.

Alembic is an optional dependency (pip install msflib[migrations] or add alembic to the app). It is only imported when a migration actually runs.

docs.title: MigrationError
docs.text:
Bases: RuntimeError

The database cannot be migrated as configured (configuration or state problems).

Also raised for Alembic's own command failures. Errors raised by a revision itself, or by the database driver while it runs (sqlalchemy.exc.DBAPIError, anything a revision raises), are not wrapped: they propagate unchanged, after the migration has been rolled back.

docs.title: MigrationConfig(metadata: MetaData, script_location: str | Path, baseline_revision: str | None = None, fresh_database: Literal['create_all', 'upgrade'] = 'create_all', advisory_lock_id: int = DEFAULT_ADVISORY_LOCK_ID) dataclass
docs.text:
What migrate needs to know about an application.

Attributes:

Name Type Description metadata MetaData

the application's SQLAlchemy metadata (all models must be imported).

script_location str | Path

the Alembic script directory (the one with env.py and versions/).

baseline_revision str | None

revision that databases without version tracking are assumed to match. Required only if such databases exist.

fresh_database Literal['create_all', 'upgrade']

what to do with an empty database. "create_all" (default) builds the tables from the metadata and stamps head, which skips migration-only operations; "upgrade" runs the whole migration chain instead.

docs.title: run_alembic_env(context: Any, target_metadata: MetaData, *, database_url: Any = None, compare_type: bool = True, **configure_kwargs: Any) -> None
docs.text:
The body of an application's alembic/env.py.

Runs on the connection that :func:migrate provides, so the schema changes, the version stamp and the advisory lock share one transaction. Standalone alembic commands (autogenerate, manual upgrades) still work: they use database_url, or sqlalchemy.url from alembic.ini.

env.py::

from alembic import context
from msflib.db.migrations import run_alembic_env
from sqlmodel import SQLModel
from app import models  # noqa: F401  (registers the tables)
from app.core.config import settings

run_alembic_env(context, SQLModel.metadata, database_url=settings.database_url)

Attach a relationship to this model after class definition.

This wraps Mapper.add_property() so callers can avoid importing SQLAlchemy internals directly in application code.

Preferred SQLModel-style usage is to provide target and link_model for many-to-many relations and let SQLAlchemy infer joins from foreign keys. secondary/primaryjoin/secondaryjoin remain available for advanced SQLAlchemy overrides.

docs.title: msflib.scope
docs.text:
Unified scope system for MSFLib.

Provides a canonical, extensible scope model for multi-tenant data access control.

ScopeCompiler handles generic scope transformations (to string, segments, or mapping). Domain-specific transformations (e.g., checkpoint keys, retrieval filters, storage keys) belong in the subsystem classes that use them (e.g., CheckpointScope, factories).

Quick start::

from msflib.scope import (
    ScopeEnvelope,
    PrincipalContext,
    ScopeCompiler,
    DimensionRegistry,
    create_default_registry,
)

registry = create_default_registry()
compiler = ScopeCompiler(registry=registry)

envelope = ScopeEnvelope(
    dimensions={"tenant_id": "42", "workspace_id": "7"},
    principal=PrincipalContext(account_id="user-1"),
)

# Compile to canonical scope string
scope_string = compiler.compile_scope_string(envelope, operation="retrieval.search")

# Compile to canonical scope segments tuple
segments = compiler.compile_scope_segments(envelope, operation="retrieval.search")

# Compile to canonical scope mapping
scope_map = compiler.compile_scope_map(envelope, operation="retrieval.search")

docs.title: ConstraintEvaluator(constraints: list[ScopeConstraint] | None = None, enforcement_level: str = 'log-only')
docs.text:
Evaluates an ordered list of constraints and returns a composite decision.

Constraints are evaluated in order until the first deny. The enforcement_level controls what happens after that deny:

- ``log-only``: return *allow* (violations are logged but not enforced).
- ``shadow``: return *deny* (violations are logged; callers observe the
    denial without an exception being raised).
- ``enforce``: raise :class:`ConstraintViolationError` on the first deny.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default constraints list[ScopeConstraint] | None

Ordered list of :class:ScopeConstraint instances.

None enforcement_level str

One of "log-only", "shadow", "enforce". Defaults to "log-only" (D5 locked decision).

'log-only'

docs.title: last_decisions: list[ScopeDecision] property
docs.text: Return decisions from the most recent :meth:evaluate call.

docs.title: evaluate(scope: ScopeEnvelope, context: dict[str, Any] | None = None) -> ScopeDecision
docs.text:
Run all constraints in order; return first deny or final allow.

Side-effects: - Stores decisions in :attr:last_decisions for audit. - Logs violations at WARNING level. - Emits scope.decision events and records metrics for the first deny (including enforce raises) and for the final effective decision (an unconditional allow, a shadow deny, or a log-only override). A log-only override therefore emits and records both the original deny and the overridden allow.

The enforcement_level controls what happens on a deny: - log-only: Log and return allow. - shadow: Log and return deny (but do not raise). - enforce: Log and raise :class:ConstraintViolationError.

docs.title: DimensionMatchConstraint(required_match: dict[str, str] | None = None, *, constraint_name: str | None = None)
docs.text:
Checks that dimension values in the scope match those in context.

Pass required_match as a mapping of {canonical_dim_key: context_key}. If the context key is present and the scope has that dimension, the values must match exactly. Missing context keys are skipped (not treated as deny).

Example::

constraint = DimensionMatchConstraint(
    required_match={"tenant_id": "current_tenant_id"},
)

If scope.get_dim("tenant_id") != context["current_tenant_id"], the constraint returns a deny decision.

By default (fail_open=False), missing or misconfigured services fail closed (deny) for security. Set fail_open=True to allow in shadow/log-only modes when the service is unavailable (e.g., for testing or during deployment).

If no principal is attached and the scope targets a concrete workspace, this constraint denies by default to avoid unauthenticated bypasses.

docs.text:
Compile envelope through the operation profile into scope_type.

A field the profile marks required must parse to its type. A field the profile marks required-nullable keeps an explicit null as None. A field the profile leaves optional keeps an explicit null as None when it is nullable, is rejected when it is not, and takes its default when the envelope supplies no value. A dimension the profile requires (or requires as nullable) must be a field of scope_type: dropping it would widen a query. Raises :exc:~msflib.scope.errors.ProfileValidationError (a ScopeError) when the operation is unknown or the envelope holds a dimension the profile does not allow, and ScopeValidationError when a required dimension is missing, a value cannot be parsed, a field is not declared by the profile, or a declared field has no value and no default.

docs.title: get_scope_dependencies(*, get_current_tenant: Callable, get_current_workspace: Callable | None = None, get_current_active_user: Callable | None = None, get_current_account: Callable | None = None) -> DependencyNamespace
docs.text:
Return reusable FastAPI dependencies yielding the caller's ScopeEnvelope.

One factory takes the site's callables and returns a DependencyNamespace (the module deps convention, see auth.get_account_dependencies). Each member is a distinct named scope shape — pick the one matching the tiers an endpoint acts in rather than parameterizing a single dependency.

get_current_tenant resolves the caller's tenant the same way get_current_workspace/get_current_account resolve theirs: as a request-scoped FastAPI dependency returning a model instance (.id read off it below), validated at the endpoint boundary instead of a bare ambient string threaded in from deep inside action/service code. Pass msflib.tenancy.deps.get_tenant_dependencies(...).get_current_tenant, which falls back to the default tenant, so a site that does not deal with tenancy passes that. It is required: this factory makes no tenant choice of its own, and every scope below carries the resolved tenant_id.

Which identity callables to pass reduces to one question: does this site have a membership entity distinct from the account — a per-workspace row with its own status and role, resolved via auth.get_user_dependencies?

  • Yes — pass get_current_workspace + get_current_active_user. get_current_active_user is what actually verifies membership (the account_id/workspace_id join and per-workspace active/kicked/banned status live there — see auth.get_current_user); workspace resolution alone does not check it, so this pair cannot be replaced by a bare get_current_account + get_current_workspace. get_account_scope then carries all three tiers, and get_workspace_scope is also available.

  • No — pass get_current_account (from auth.get_account_dependencies — typically get_current_active_account, so an inactive account can't reach a scoped endpoint). Whether a workspace tier exists at all is then a second, independent choice:

  • No workspace concept: omit get_current_workspace. Only get_account_scope / get_tenant_scope are exposed — get_workspace_scope has no meaning without workspaces.

  • Workspace exists as an attribute of the account (e.g. an Account.current_workspace_id field), not a separate membership row: also pass get_current_workspace. get_workspace_scope becomes available too, since a workspace tier now exists — but nothing here verifies the account belongs to that workspace, because there is no membership row to check membership against.

Returns:

Type Description DependencyNamespace exposing:
  • get_account_scope — every tier the caller has (tenant + account, plus workspace when the site has one): for member-facing reads and writes where user/account-scoped rows participate.
  • get_workspace_scope — tenant + workspace, no account tier: for admin surfaces that only touch workspace-scoped rows (an account_id there would fetch user-scoped rows only to discard them). Only present when the site has a workspace tier.
  • get_tenant_scope — tenant only, for platform-level surfaces.

docs.title: DimensionMatchConstraint(required_match: dict[str, str] | None = None, *, constraint_name: str | None = None)
docs.text:
Checks that dimension values in the scope match those in context.

Pass required_match as a mapping of {canonical_dim_key: context_key}. If the context key is present and the scope has that dimension, the values must match exactly. Missing context keys are skipped (not treated as deny).

Example::

constraint = DimensionMatchConstraint(
    required_match={"tenant_id": "current_tenant_id"},
)

If scope.get_dim("tenant_id") != context["current_tenant_id"], the constraint returns a deny decision.

docs.title: MembershipConstraint(*, deny_without_principal: bool = True, fail_open: bool = False)
docs.text:
Stub: validates that the principal is a member of the scoped workspace.

Production implementations should inject a membership service or DB session via the context dict (key: membership_service).

By default (fail_open=False), missing or misconfigured services fail closed (deny) for security. Set fail_open=True to allow in shadow/log-only modes when the service is unavailable (e.g., for testing or during deployment).

If no principal is attached and the scope targets a concrete workspace, this constraint denies by default to avoid unauthenticated bypasses.

docs.title: RoleConstraint(required_role: str, *, deny_without_principal: bool = True)
docs.text:
Stub: validates that the principal has the required role.

Requires the scope envelope to carry a PrincipalContext with a roles set. The required_role is checked against principal.roles.

If no principal is attached, behaviour depends on deny_without_principal: - True (default): deny. - False: allow (useful for service-to-service calls where role is implicit).

docs.title: ChannelConstraint(required_channel: str, *, deny_without_channel: bool = True)
docs.text:
Validates that the request channel matches the required channel.

Channel is read from scope.attributes['channel'] first and falls back to context['current_channel'] when absent.

docs.title: ConstraintEvaluator(constraints: list[ScopeConstraint] | None = None, enforcement_level: str = 'log-only')
docs.text:
Evaluates an ordered list of constraints and returns a composite decision.

Constraints are evaluated in order until the first deny. The enforcement_level controls what happens after that deny:

- ``log-only``: return *allow* (violations are logged but not enforced).
- ``shadow``: return *deny* (violations are logged; callers observe the
    denial without an exception being raised).
- ``enforce``: raise :class:`ConstraintViolationError` on the first deny.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default constraints list[ScopeConstraint] | None

Ordered list of :class:ScopeConstraint instances.

None enforcement_level str

One of "log-only", "shadow", "enforce". Defaults to "log-only" (D5 locked decision).

'log-only'

docs.title: last_decisions: list[ScopeDecision] property
docs.text: Return decisions from the most recent :meth:evaluate call.

docs.title: evaluate(scope: ScopeEnvelope, context: dict[str, Any] | None = None) -> ScopeDecision
docs.text:
Run all constraints in order; return first deny or final allow.

Side-effects: - Stores decisions in :attr:last_decisions for audit. - Logs violations at WARNING level. - Emits scope.decision events and records metrics for the first deny (including enforce raises) and for the final effective decision (an unconditional allow, a shadow deny, or a log-only override). A log-only override therefore emits and records both the original deny and the overridden allow.

The enforcement_level controls what happens on a deny: - log-only: Log and return allow. - shadow: Log and return deny (but do not raise). - enforce: Log and raise :class:ConstraintViolationError.

A profile defines the required/optional dimensions and policy-level enforcement settings for a named operation. The compiler validates envelopes against profiles before compiling.

Scope dimensions are registered at application start-up. The registry can be locked (via :meth:lock) to prevent further registrations at runtime; locking is optional and caller-controlled.

docs.text:
Central registry of scope dimension specifications.

Usage::

registry = DimensionRegistry()
registry.register(DimensionSpec(canonical_key="project_id", priority=25))
registry.lock()

docs.title: ScopeFactory(compiler: ScopeCompiler)
docs.text: Builds typed scope dataclasses from envelopes, validated by an operation profile.

docs.title: build(envelope: ScopeEnvelope, scope_type: type[TypedScope], *, operation: str) -> TypedScope
docs.text:
Compile envelope through the operation profile into scope_type.

A field the profile marks required must parse to its type. A field the profile marks required-nullable keeps an explicit null as None. A field the profile leaves optional keeps an explicit null as None when it is nullable, is rejected when it is not, and takes its default when the envelope supplies no value. A dimension the profile requires (or requires as nullable) must be a field of scope_type: dropping it would widen a query. Raises :exc:~msflib.scope.errors.ProfileValidationError (a ScopeError) when the operation is unknown or the envelope holds a dimension the profile does not allow, and ScopeValidationError when a required dimension is missing, a value cannot be parsed, a field is not declared by the profile, or a declared field has no value and no default.

docs.title: is_production_db(db_url: str) -> bool
docs.text:
Whether a database URL must be treated as sensitive (conservative heuristic).

Only a SQLite file under ./tmp/ or /tmp/ is local. The path is normalised before it is compared, so sqlite:///./tmp/../prod.db (which SQLite resolves to ./prod.db) is not mistaken for a temp file, a path containing a backslash is never local, and symlinks are followed: a link inside the temp directory that points elsewhere makes the file sensitive. Everything else, including in-memory SQLite and every non-SQLite URL (also PostgreSQL on localhost), is sensitive.

docs.text:
Handles database seeding by running seeders defined in a YAML configuration file.

The SeedRunner loads seeder configurations, processes record data, dynamically imports custom seeder classes, actions, and models, and executes seeding operations into the database. It also allows selective execution of seeders for specific models.

Shared context storing seeds and cumulative stats.

Seeder configurations parsed from the seeders YAML file.

data_paths list[str]

Directory paths where seeder data files are searched.

models_to_seed list[str]

Optional list of model names to restrict seeding to. If None, all seeders defined in the YAML file will be executed.

Flag to enable/disable seeding logs.

Stores statistics about the seeding process.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default seeders_yml_path str

Path to the seeders YAML configuration file. Defaults to "./app/seed/seeders.yml".

required data_path str

Path to the default directory containing seed data files.

None data_paths list[str]

Additional directories containing seed data files. Defaults to "./app/seed/data".

None models_to_seed list[str]

None show_log bool

Whether to log seeding operations. Defaults to True.

docs.text:
Run all seeders defined in the YAML configuration against the given database engine.

This method
  1. Opens a database session.
  2. Collects seeding statistics.
  3. Iterates over all configured seeders.
  4. For each seeder:
    • Loads associated records from YAML/JSON/CSV files if defined.
    • Validates the configuration schema.
    • Runs either:
      • A custom seeder class (subclass of SeederBase).
      • An action-based seeder.

A SQLAlchemy engine connected to the target database.

docs.title: msflib.tree
docs.text:
msflib.tree — closure-table tree utilities.

Provides: - ClosureMixin — adds parent_id and position to a node model. - make_closure_table(name, node_table) — creates the paired closure model. - TreeAction — tree operations (create_child, update, move, reorder, delete, list_ancestors, list_descendants, list_subtree_ids, get_depth, get_path) that maintain closure rows inside the caller's transaction. Composes ActionMixin and has no generic create or bulk delete. Pure SQL; SQLite-safe.

docs.title: TreeAction
docs.text:
Bases: ActionMixin[NodeType, CreateSchemaType, UpdateSchemaType]

Closure-table tree operations that keep ancestor rows consistent.

Composes ActionMixin (reads, lifecycle events, write primitives) and exposes its own write surface: create_child, update, move, reorder and delete. There is no plain create or bulk delete, since either would bypass closure maintenance.

Subclasses must set _closure_model to the model returned by make_closure_table::

class StructureAction(TreeAction[LearningStructureNode, ...]):
    _closure_model = StructureClosure

parent_id and position are structural: they are set by create_child, move and reorder only, so the create and update schemas must not declare them.

Mutation methods flush closure changes inside the caller's transaction. create_child, move and reorder default to commit=False so the caller owns the commit.

docs.title: update(session: Session, *, model: NodeType, data: UpdateSchemaType, commit: bool = True) -> NodeType
docs.text: Apply the fields set on data; reparenting and ordering use move/reorder.

docs.title: create_child(session: Session, *, data: CreateSchemaType, parent_id: int | None, position: int = 0, update: dict[str, Any] | None = None, commit: bool = False) -> NodeType
docs.text:
Create a node under parent_id (None for a root) with its closure rows.

update carries server-derived fields; parent_id and position always win.

docs.title: list_ancestors(session: Session, node_id: int, *, include_self: bool = False) -> list[NodeType]
docs.text:
Return ancestor nodes, nearest-first (parent before grandparent).

When include_self is True the node itself is appended at the end (depth 0, after all proper ancestors).

docs.title: list_descendants(session: Session, node_id: int, *, include_self: bool = False, max_depth: int | None = None) -> list[NodeType]
docs.text: Return all descendant nodes in breadth-first order.

docs.title: list_subtree_ids(session: Session, node_id: int, *, include_self: bool = True) -> list[int]
docs.text: Return all descendant ids (no DB round-trip for models).

docs.title: get_depth(session: Session, node_id: int) -> int
docs.text: Return the depth of node_id from the root (root = 0).

docs.title: get_path(session: Session, node_id: int, *, include_self: bool = False) -> list[NodeType]
docs.text: Return the ancestor chain nearest-first, optionally appending the node itself at the end (path[-1] == node when include_self=True).

docs.title: move(session: Session, node_id: int, new_parent_id: int | None, *, new_position: int | None = None, commit: bool = False) -> NodeType
docs.text:
Move node_id (and its entire subtree) under new_parent_id.

Raises ValueError if new_parent_id is a descendant of node_id (would create a cycle).

docs.title: reorder(session: Session, parent_id: int | None, ordered_ids: list[int], *, commit: bool = False) -> None
docs.text:
Set the position of direct children of parent_id to match ordered_ids (0-based index in the list).

ordered_ids must list every direct child of parent_id exactly once.

docs.title: ClosureMixin
docs.text:
Mix into a SQLModel(table=True) node class.

Adds: - parent_id: int | None — FK referencing the same table; None for roots. Declared as a plain indexed nullable column (no SQLModel FK macro) so the mixin stays table-agnostic; subclasses or TreeAction set up the FK themselves via Field(foreign_key=…) in the concrete model. - position: int — 0-based sibling order; unique enforcement is left to the concrete model or to TreeAction.reorder.

docs.title: make_closure_table(name: str, node_table: type) -> type
docs.text:
Return a new SQLModel closure-table class paired with node_table.

The closure table has three columns: - ancestor_id — int FK to node_table. - descendant_id — int FK to node_table. - depth — 0 for the self-reference row, 1 for parent→child, …

The composite PK is (ancestor_id, descendant_id).

name becomes the __tablename__ and the Python class name is derived from it (e.g. "learning_structure_closure" → LearningStructureClosure).

Usage::

StructureClosure = make_closure_table(
    "learning_structure_closure",
    LearningStructureNode,
)
